https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/traitors-.text: Jordan Lloyd Beck Sun, August 23, 2026 at 5:51 PM UTC 0 Freddie Fraser has revealed his new relationship -Credit:BBC Traitors star Freddie Fraser has been supported by fans after coming out and announcing his relationship. The reality star, 22, found fame when he competed on the third series of Claudia Winkleman's BBC hit , which aired in early 2025 and was eventually won by Jake Brown Leanne Quigley. Over the weekend, former politics student Freddie took to social media to announce that he is in a relationship with model Bailey Ramsden, and posted a black-and-white photo strip of them both. He simply captioned the post with a heart, but several of the TV star's followers were quick to congratulate him over the happy news. One said: "LOVEEEEE!!!! SO CUTE," and another wrote: "Gorgeous, so happy for you." Coronation Street stars 'didn't drink water for two days' ahead of naked scenes Our Yorkshire Farm's Clive Owen reflects on farm's future as he marks 'last day' Freddie shot to fame on the third series of The Traitors -Credit:Getty Images He reveled the news with a romantic post on Instagram -Credit:@freddiefraserr/Instagram A third wrote: "this is the best news xx" Amanda Lovett, who appeared on the first series of The Traitors, said: "Aww I’m so happy for you," whilst former X Factor star Jack Remmington simply left a string of heart-faced emojis. Freddie, who before finding television fame was a top-ranked sprint hurdle athlete in the years before he signed up for The Traitors , was a Faithful on the BBC show before being recruited as a Traitor by Charlotte Berman in episode 10. But in a shock twist, he was banished from the castle following a slip up involving Minah Shannon less than a day later, and hastily exited the castle. When he was banished - and had to reveal he was a Traitor - he told the group it had been “the honour of my life” to take part in the TV series. Since then, he has carved out a successful career as an influencer, with a combined following count of almost 250,000 across various social media platforms. The star memorably entered the castle as a Faithful but was banished shortly after becoming a Traitor -Credit:BBC His new relationship comes more than a year after it was reported that he had split from Nisha Davenport, whom he had met at university, and it was claimed that his new career had made it tricky to keep things going. A source told The Sun : "Freddie quietly split from Nisha earlier this year, shortly after a loved-up trip to Budapest. She’d been by his side throughout his Traitors fame but Freddie soon found himself living a showbiz lifestyle that he’d always dreamed of. “They were also both incredibly aware that after university it would be more difficult than ever to keep the romance going strong. The split was very amicable and there was no drama on either side”. * Follow Mirror Celebs and TV on TikTok , Snapchat , Instagram , Twitter , Facebook , YouTube and Threads . https://www.texarkanagazette.com/news/20.text: NATO jets shoot down drone over Lithuania and Russian ship fires flares at Danish helicopter VILNIUS, Lithuania -- NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace overnight, officials said Tuesday, the day after the head of the alliance said strikes close to its territory would only increase its support for Ukraine in the war against Russia's full-scale invasion. Military officials in Lithuania, a NATO member, said the incident marked the first time that a drone had been shot down in its airspace. Authorities didn't comment on the drone's origin or purpose, saying further investigation was needed, but two senior officials said the device was likely carrying explosives. Officials in other NATO countries, including Germany, Denmark, the United Kingdom and Poland, have in recent weeks accused Russia of involvement in acts such as drone incursions, sabotage, arson and surveillance of defense facilities and in plans to use a drone carrying explosives to attack an airport. Separately, Denmark said Tuesday that one of its air force helicopters was fired on with flares as it was carrying out surveillance of a Russian frigate in the Baltic Sea. Strikes close to NATO territory showed Russian President Vladimir Putin's "desperation and also his desire to sow fear and terror," NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said Monday. He spoke after a Russian drone struck a railway line near the Ukraine-Poland border on Sunday shortly after senior visiting officials passed through. Rutte pledged to bolster the 32-nation alliance's own defenses along its long eastern border with Russia and with Belarus, a Russian ally. Ursula von der Leyen, head of the European Commission, said the incidents in Lithuania and Denmark were not isolated but "part of a broader pattern of Russian aggression and provocation against Europe, testing our readiness and our resolve." "Russia will find our resolve only growing stronger," she said. DRONE FOUND TO BE CARRYING EXPLOSIVES The drone downed Tuesday in Lithuania fell near the village of Pratkūnai, about 60 miles (100 kilometers) west of the capital, Vilnius, and near the Kaunas Reservoir, Lithuania's National Crisis Management Center said Tuesday. Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of the crisis center, told Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT that the drone most likely entered from Belarus. It remained in Lithuanian airspace for about 30 minutes and flew along the outskirts of populated areas before being intercepted, he said. Writing on Facebook on Tuesday, Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said an explosive device was detected on the drone and neutralized by bomb-disposal experts. Menacing drones have repeatedly loomed over the skies of Lithuania, which shares borders with Belarus and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. In May, residents of Vilnius were told to take shelter, and the president and prime minister were taken to safe locations during an alarm over drone activity near the border with Belarus. Stray Ukrainian drones have also previously crossed the border into Baltic airspace, including in May, when a NATO fighter jet shot down a Ukrainian drone over southern Estonia. Meanwhile, Denmark accused Russia of firing flares at one of its air force helicopters in connection with "routine photographic coverage" of a Russian frigate in waters off the port of Gedser in the Baltic Sea. "This is completely unacceptable," the Danish Foreign Ministry wrote on X, saying that the Russian ambassador was summoned over the incident. Russia's ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, said it was "not the first time" that Danish air force helicopters "carried out dangerous maneuvers near Russian warships." He said the Danish helicopter conducted "provocative actions against the Russian frigate." The Kremlin declined to comment Tuesday, with presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov saying that he did not have details. KYIV SAYS IT'S 'READY TO SUPPORT DE-ESCALATION' In Ukraine, Russian drone strikes continued across the country following a social media post from U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed "not to hit" each other's energy infrastructure. Trump didn't offer details on the purported agreement. Previous efforts to broker even a partial ceasefire have repeatedly fallen apart within hours, with both sides accusing the other of violations. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said late Monday that Kyiv was "ready to support de-escalation" if the United States could ensure "Russia is genuinely ready to stop this war." But Zelenskyy said Tuesday in a statement that Moscow had continued to attack Ukraine's energy sector, logistics and critical infrastructure, and that Kyiv responded by striking an oil refinery in Syzran, a city in western Russia. "There is no alternative to ending this war. And all forms of pressure on Russia must create the right diplomatic conditions," Zelenskyy said. The Kremlin said Tuesday that it considered Trump's proposal for a ceasefire on energy infrastructure to be "a good idea." However, it stressed that strikes on Russian oil refineries were not the root cause of global supply issues for gas or diesel. "The core problem lies in the export of petroleum products to global markets," Peskov said. He said that countries instead needed to guarantee safe navigation for oil tankers and lift global sanctions on Russian oil. The Kremlin's comments contradict those of Trump, who on Sunday called on Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and claimed that such attacks had caused a global shortage. "Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Trump told reporters, following news on Friday that diesel prices in the U.S. had soared past an average of $6 a gallon. "We spoke to Mr. Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don't hit diesel fuel, because that's hurting, that's hurting the world," he said. Ukraine's State Emergency Service said Tuesday that Russian strikes on Kyiv had killed one person and wounded seven other people since the start of the day, with attacks carried out on the capital's gas stations. Two more people were killed in separate Russian strikes in the Ukrainian cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, the emergency service said. Elsewhere, Russian forces shot down 222 Ukrainian drones overnight, Russia's Defense Ministry said Tuesday. A "massive" Ukrainian drone attack sparked several fires in the Russian city of Taganrog, regional Gov. Yuri Slyusar said. He said on Telegram that two apartment buildings and three private homes had been damaged, as well as an educational institution, agricultural warehouses and a site belonging to Russian e-retailer Ozon. Zelenskyy said Tuesday that Kyiv's forces had targeted a drone-production facility in the city. UKRAINIAN PARLIAMENT VOTES TO DISMISS PROSECUTOR GENERAL In other developments, Ukraine's parliament voted to dismiss Ruslan Kravchenko from the post of prosecutor general Tuesday. Kravchenko submitted his resignation on Sept. 7 amid an investigation into corruption in his office, though no notice of suspicion was issued against him. Zelenskyy had suspended Kravchenko from the post the day before. Kravchenko had served as prosecutor general since June 21, 2025. Repeated corruption scandals have hurt Zelenskyy's approval ratings. ------ Associated Press writer Hanna Arhirova contributed to this report from Kyiv, Ukraine. Image: Sarah Meyssonnier/REUTERS Advertisement Over 400 schools and colleges across France remained closed on Friday as student protests over education-related grievances continued — with some turning violent. "There are over ⁠400 schools and other educational establishments that I know of that will be closed," confirmed French Education ​Minister Edouard Geffray on broadcaster ​ France 2 late on Thursday night. The protests ​against teacher shortages, dilapidated school buildings and a lack of learning materials erupted at lycées (equivalent to US high schools) in the Paris region last month before spreading across the country this week. Students are angry at what they see as a general lack of investment in their education Image: Abdul Saboor/REUTERS Student protests in France: damage, injuries, arrests Police have made around 2,000 arrests and scores of people have been injured, including 40 high school principals, according to Geffray. Fires were started in at least two high schools on Thursday, while teachers were reportedly inadvertently ​splashed with petrol ⁠at a third in the southern city of Marseille, according to officials. At ​least one car was torched in the eastern city of Strasbourg while riot police clashed with youths in Toulouse in the southwest. In the southeastern region of Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, authorities claimed that "at least €25 million" of damage has been done in their jurisdiction alone. On Friday, more clashes between student protesters and police were reported in cities across the country, including in Loire, where several officers were injured, and in the capital Paris. But students have also criticized what they see as a heavy-handed police response. "You don't want to hear our words; you just fire tear gas," one student wrote on a placard outside the Lycée Voltaire in central Paris (see main photo above). "Protest is a fundamental right," read another sign. France students protest school conditions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Minister Geffray told broadcasters on Friday morning that "violent individuals" were "infiltrating groups of students" and "taking the movement hostage" and called on parents to prevent their children from joining the protests. "What matters now is ensuring our children are no longer out on the streets, because they are in danger," he said. Geffray was planning to meet with student representatives and trade unions on Friday, saying: "Today will be a day of dialogue." France: government blames far-left LFI According to Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, French domestic intelligence agencies told a crisis meeting on Thursday that the movement has been initiated by politicians from the left-wing party La France Insoumise (France Unbowed or LFI) – who have denied the allegations. Veteran LFI leader and 2027 presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has indeed supported the protests but called on students to use non-violent methods. "Students, teachers and educational staff are facing the same state of neglect and their positions and claims should be respected," he wrote in a statement earlier this week, calling for "disciplined struggle, no panic, no irritation." Meanwhile, student union bodies have called for a day of mass protest next Tuesday, October 6, under the slogan: "Police out of schools! No to the repression of student mobilization!" "The police have no place in front of educational establishments," read a statement. "We support the ongoing mobilization and call for it to be reinforced." https://www.dw.com/en/south-sudan-s-road.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Nq5K South Sudan became a sovereign state on July 9, 2011 Image: picture-alliance/dpa Advertisement South Sudan has scheduled a general election for December 22, the first since the country gained independence from Sudan in 2011. But as preparations lag, political tensions are high and the debate has intensified since President Salva Kiir dissolved the transitional unity government on September 22 to form a caretaker administration. Denis Logonyi, a journalist based in the capital of South Sudan Juba, said that many in the country, which has seen violent power struggles and political instability, were not only concerned about the logistics of the polls. Will elections happen in South Sudan? To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 audio "People have different views on these elections," he told DW. "You hear discussions in political circles and on social media, but ordinary people are not talking much about them." One voter complained that "there has been no voter education, no voter registration, and only a few months remain." Another told DW that while South Sudanese citizens were eager for a credible election process, the country was not adequately prepared. Food prices are rising, civil servants are not being paid, and displaced people are struggling, they said. Politicians admit to 'obstacles' but agree to adhere to election timeline Political parties have until October 22 to present their manifestos and register. On October 7, South Sudan concluded a two-week Inter-Party Dialogue, in which 39 parties participated, discussing key issues ahead of the election. Logonyi said that some civil society groups had been left out of the dialogue, which was initiated by President Kiir. Minister of Cabinet Affairs Martin Elia Lomuro outlined a few of the challenges: "Delayed funding could severely affect civic education and election infrastructure. There is a need for a clear legal framework to govern the participation of the country's administrative areas. The three administrative areas are not clearly reflected in the National Election Act, which is necessary for the election outcomes to be accepted." He added that "a credible election requires security readiness throughout the entire cycle — including campaign rallies, polling stations, voting, counting, and results transmission. The unified security forces have not yet been fully deployed." According to Albino Akol Atak, the deputy rapporteur of the Inter-Party Dialogue and minister of humanitarian affairs and disaster management, the parties unanimously agreed to adhere to the election timeline. "The election train has left the station, and it has no reverse gear," he said. "We are trying to smooth the pathway for this train to arrive on December 22, 2026, without obstacles." Meanwhile, Changkuoth Bichok Reath, the secretary general of the South Sudan Opposition Alliance (SSOA), said he strongly believed "that successfully conducting the election on December 22 requires coordinated, inclusive action from all national institutions, political parties, security actors, civil society, and other stakeholders." He added that "given the limited time remaining, priority should be placed on resolving outstanding legal issues and ensuring constructive dialogue among political actors. Furthermore, political parties must be funded to meet key requirements, because a lack of funding will only draw us backward." South Sudan's checkered election history South Sudan has endured decades of conflict, from long wars that preceded independence to a devastating civil war that erupted just two years after it became a sovereign state. Power-sharing transitional governments have been in place under fragile peace deals, including the Revitalized Peace Agreement of September 2018 . Elections have repeatedly been planned then put off. South Sudanese President Salva Kiir is set to contest the December election Image: Brian Inganga/AP Photo/picture alliance Armed opposition groups remain active, and many citizens fear political tensions could trigger renewed violence. "The absence of [former Vice President] Riek Machar from the political process is a major concern," Logonyi said. "If there is to be an election or a meaningful political dialogue, many believe he has to be part of it." In 2018, a power-sharing deal that saw Kiir become president and Machar — his long-time rival and main opposition leader — vice president briefly stabilized the country. However, tensions between the two men persisted and in March 2025, Machar was placed under house arrest. He was later put on trial for offences that include treason and murder . South Sudan's former vice president, Riek Machar, pictured in court in Juba in September 2025 Image: Peter Louis Gume/AFP Key conditions for elections not fulfilled yet "The government has demonstrated that it is keen for the election to happen," said Wambui Njehu Nzigo, an analyst with Control Risks, a global consulting firm. "But there are important processes that have not yet taken place." The lack of voter registration is among the biggest concerns. "If elections are to take place soon, you would expect there already to be a voter register," Nzigo said. "There is very little time for that to happen." Security reforms required under the 2018 peace deal have not yet been finished. These include the unification of armed groups to create the conditions for a stable transition. Analysts have long warned that if these key issues are not addressed the legitimacy of any election would be undermined. "The elections would be taking place in an environment where there is still active fighting in some parts of the country," Nzigo said. "The fact that the main opposition leader is under house arrest raises questions about whether this will be a true competition." According to Logonyi, civil society groups are calling for greater dialogue, political inclusion and protections for journalists and activists before the vote is held. How instability persists in South Sudan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Ongoing flooding could interfere with the vote Futhermore, South Sudan faces severe flooding, a displacement crisis and food insecurity. This could make it difficult for some citizens to reach polling stations, Nzigo said. For those displaced by conflict, there's uncertainty over how they can register and cast their ballots. Floodwaters, oil and health fears in South Sudan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Experts warn that a vote without broad participation could lead to a disputed outcome and instensify conflict. Regional organizations such as the African Union and international partners are expected to continue encouraging an inclusive political process. Analysts argue that the focus should be not only on ensuring elections take place, but also on creating conditions that make them credible. For many South Sudanese, the choice is clear: elections alone won't guarantee stability. This article contains material generated by artificial intelligence (AI) from the AfricaLink podcast. Photograph: Friso Gentsch/EPA View image in fullscreen Audi’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a rally on Saturday to announce the factory in Macon, Georgia. Photograph: Friso Gentsch/EPA Volkswagen (VW) Volkswagen to build $4bn Audi SUV factory in US despite job cuts at home VW investment, creating 4,500 jobs in Georgia, comes amid Trump’s damaging tariffs, intense Chinese competition and costly shift towards EVs Jasper Jolly and agencies Sun 25 Oct 2026 09.43 EDT Last modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 10.27 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Audi has said it will spend $4bn (£3bn) to build its first factory in the US, as its parent company, Volkswagen, struggles with the impact of steep tariffs imposed by Donald Trump. The German brand’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a campaign rally on Saturday night to announce the factory in Macon, Georgia , in an unusual move by a big European brand just days before the US midterm elections. The Republican party under Trump is trying to retain control of both houses of Congress, but it is polling poorly as it struggles with higher fuel prices caused by Trump’s war on Iran , as well as his trade war against some of the US’s biggest trading partners. Volkswagen to cut further 50,000 jobs as it ends row with union over revival plan Read more Trump has long tried to convince voters that his tariffs are helping to increase the number of manufacturing jobs in the US, and has seized on any new factory investments. However, US vehicle and parts employment has fallen since Trump took office last year. Audi, Volkswagen’s most important premium brand, has suffered from Trump’s 15% tariffs on imports from the EU as well as the president’s efforts to cut sales of battery electric vehicles in favour of petrol cars. It said it aims to build 200,000 SUVs at the new US factory, creating 4,500 jobs. The factory will build the Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, shifting some production from Bratislava in Slovakia. Volkswagen has said Trump’s tariffs cost it up to €5bn(£4.2bn)a year, before the impact of lower sales. The German manufacturer this month said it was still struggling with “continued high pressure from import tariffs”. The carmaker was also forced to shift some production of its cheapest cars, such as the Jetta saloon and Taos SUV, from Mexico to the US. The new factory may add to tensions in Germany, where Volkswagen has started to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories . It has blamed the job losses on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as the tariffs and a need to invest heavily in the shift to EVs for markets other than the US. Döllner said he accepted the invitation to speak at Trump’s rally out of respect for the US. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion “We are planning to bring our ⁠biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” he said at the event. “This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market.” Volkswagen’s chief executive, Oliver Blume, told investors in July that “US tariffs create a significant burden and restrict international trade”. However, the group has said there is still demand in the US for Audi’s large petrol SUVs, and it is planning its largest-ever SUV, the Q9, with the American market in mind. Large petrol-powered SUVs have played a big role in global carbon emissions .
